slides.0.title: Geography, Climate and Soils
slides.0.subtitle: Lake effect, winter injury, and the Okanagan's rain shadow and dry climate
slides.1.title: Latitude and a cool climate
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Latitudes of the main regions
slides.1.highlights.0.content: The Vineland station in Niagara is at about 43°11'N; Lake Erie North Shore, near 42°N, has the most heat units of Ontario's viticultural areas; Prince Edward County, at 44°N, is Ontario's most northerly appellation; BC's vineyards lie at about 49–50°N (AWRI, Wine With Seth)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: A cool-climate country
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The Canadian Encyclopedia treats Canada as a cool-climate wine country, comparable to New Zealand, northern France, Italy and Germany
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Cold injury is the main limit
slides.1.highlights.2.content: AWRI says severe cold injury and spring frost are the major factors limiting viticulture in this part of Ontario; an extreme cold event in early 2024 left many BC vineyards unable to produce a crop that year (AWRI, Wine With Seth)
slides.1.content: Latitude is moderate; it is the continental winter that bites.
slides.2.title: Ontario: lakes and escarpment
slides.2.highlights.0.title: The lake effect
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Lakes Ontario and Erie moderate winter temperatures and bring cool onshore breezes in summer, with Lake Ontario's influence the stronger; the breezes also delay bud development until spring frost danger passes (AWRI, Wine With Seth)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: The Niagara Escarpment
slides.2.highlights.1.content: The escarpment encourages onshore winds that dissipate fog and reduce frost risk. Heights differ by source: AWRI describes a 60–100 m ridge 5–20 km south of the lakeshore, while Wine With Seth gives about 177 m at most, so the figure is not tested
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Soils and drainage
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Niagara's soils are a mix of clay, clay-loam, loam and sand deposited when the escarpment was an ancient lakeshore; with high rainfall (about 498 mm in the growing season and 860 mm a year) and poorly drained clay, most vineyards install tile drains in every first or second row (AWRI, an older source)
slides.2.content: In Ontario, the lakes keep winter from being too cold.
slides.3.title: British Columbia: dry in the rain shadow
slides.3.highlights.0.title: The Okanagan rain shadow
slides.3.highlights.0.content: The Okanagan lies in the rain shadow of the Coast Mountains and Cascades: the coast gets 60+ inches a year but the Okanagan only about 10–12 inches. Rainfall falls from about 400 mm in the north (near Vernon) to about 250–300 mm at Osoyoos (Wine With Seth); the south is semi-desert and needs irrigation (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: A valley 175 km long
slides.3.highlights.1.content: The Okanagan runs about 175 km from Vernon to Osoyoos at the US border; Okanagan Lake itself is about 135 km long, followed by Skaha, Vaseux and Osoyoos lakes. The north is cool-continental and the south semi-arid (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Diurnal range
slides.3.highlights.2.content: In the south summer afternoon highs reach 30–35°C with diurnal shifts of 15–20°C; the valley floor sits at about 280–340 m and bench vineyards at about 300–600 m (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.content: BC relies on dryness and diurnal range, not on a lake-moderated winter.
